paragraphs: South Louisiana turf-insect service

Fast thinning, chewed blades, yellow patches, or disturbed soil may point to chinch bugs, armyworms, sod webworms, mole crickets, or another turf pest. Grow Green evaluates the evidence before recommending a targeted response.
An insecticide can suppress a susceptible target pest when the timing and application fit. It cannot revive turf tissue or roots that are already dead.
Evidence before application

Useful clues come from where the injury begins, what part of the plant is damaged, whether insects are present, and how conditions changed. The border between healthy and injured turf is often more informative than the dead-looking center.
Common local suspects
These are scouting clues—not a diagnosis from the screen. Pest species, life stage, population, weather, and turf condition affect whether treatment is justified.
Small sap-feeding insects strongly associated with St. Augustinegrass. Their injury can resemble drought and often begins in stressed, sunny areas.
Caterpillars that feed on grass blades and can remove foliage rapidly during an outbreak. Most turfgrasses can be affected; bermudagrass is a common target in Louisiana.
Larvae feed on leaf tissue, often making affected turf appear unevenly clipped or scalped. St. Augustine, bermuda, and centipede are common hosts in Louisiana.
Some species feed on turf while tunneling can also loosen soil, dry roots, and disrupt the surface. Timing and life stage strongly affect treatment strategy.

Other Louisiana turf pests—including spittlebugs and white grubs—can create yellowing, thinning, or root injury. The treatment target should match what is actually present, not simply the most familiar pest name.
Real lawn. Real field evidence.

This short walkthrough shows armyworm injury on an actual local St. Augustine lawn. It demonstrates why blade-level inspection matters when a lawn appears to thin suddenly—but similar-looking damage still needs its own evaluation.
The wrong treatment delays the right correction. These problems can overlap with or closely resemble insect injury.
Large Patch, Take-All Root Rot, Gray Leaf Spot, and other diseases can produce brown, yellow, or thinning turf without an insect being the primary cause.
Missed zones, clogged heads, poor coverage, and heat stress can closely mimic chinch-bug injury—especially in full sun and near hard surfaces.
Scalping, dull blades, spills, overlap, drift, or a recent product application can leave patterns that appear suddenly without turf-feeding insects.
Compaction, drainage, construction debris, buried material, thatch, shade, or root disease may weaken turf and alter how firmly it is anchored.
The target pest, life stage, location in the turf, and severity help determine whether treatment makes sense and what follow-up may be needed.
Share the grass type, where damage began, how fast it moved, what you see in the blades or soil, and anything already applied.
We compare the injury with likely insects, disease, irrigation, mowing, and root stress. The active edge often receives the closest look.
When an actionable pest is present or strongly supported, we choose a labeled product and application approach appropriate for that pest and site.
We explain watering, mowing, and monitoring steps. Follow-up depends on pest biology, life stage, pressure, weather, and surviving turf.
Once feeding pressure is reduced, the lawn still needs viable crowns or runners, suitable growing weather, water, and time to replace lost tissue.
Choose the right outdoor service
Fire ants and biting pests need different programs. Use the closest service below, or choose “not sure” in the form.
Chinch bugs, armyworms, sod webworms, mole crickets, and other pests damaging grass blades, roots, or soil.
Visible mounds, colony activity, and stinging fire ants across lawns, play areas, and other treatable outdoor spaces.
Biting-pest pressure around shaded foliage, resting sites, lawn edges, and the outdoor areas your household uses.

Common local suspects

Different pests leave different evidence.

These are scouting clues—not a diagnosis from the screen. Pest species, life stage, population, weather, and turf condition affect whether treatment is justified.

Adult southern chinch bug
Hot-weather concern

Southern Chinch Bugs

Small sap-feeding insects strongly associated with St. Augustinegrass. Their injury can resemble drought and often begins in stressed, sunny areas.

  • Yellow-to-brown patches that can expand outward
  • Activity near the border of injured and healthy turf
  • Tiny red-orange nymphs or black-and-white adults may be present
Leaf-feeding caterpillar pattern
Usually summer into fall

Fall Armyworms

Caterpillars that feed on grass blades and can remove foliage rapidly during an outbreak. Most turfgrasses can be affected; bermudagrass is a common target in Louisiana.

  • Chewed, skeletonized, thinned, or bare-looking turf
  • Larvae may be more active morning or after dark
  • Green pellets or concentrated bird activity may be clues
Short, ragged, or scalped-looking blades
Mid-summer into early fall

Tropical Sod Webworms

Larvae feed on leaf tissue, often making affected turf appear unevenly clipped or scalped. St. Augustine, bermuda, and centipede are common hosts in Louisiana.

  • Ragged leaf edges or noticeably shorter turf
  • Yellow or brown patches as feeding intensifies
  • Larvae often feed at night and shelter lower in the turf
Turf damage still requires pest confirmation
Soil and root injury

Mole Crickets

Some species feed on turf while tunneling can also loosen soil, dry roots, and disrupt the surface. Timing and life stage strongly affect treatment strategy.

  • Small raised tunnels or loosened, disturbed soil
  • Weak turf with clipped roots or poor anchoring
  • Damage may be patchy and easier to confirm with a close inspection

Other Louisiana turf pests—including spittlebugs and white grubs—can create yellowing, thinning, or root injury. The treatment target should match what is actually present, not simply the most familiar pest name.

When lawn insecticide is not the first answer.

The wrong treatment delays the right correction. These problems can overlap with or closely resemble insect injury.

Explore lawn fungus control

Lawn disease

Large Patch, Take-All Root Rot, Gray Leaf Spot, and other diseases can produce brown, yellow, or thinning turf without an insect being the primary cause.

Drought or irrigation gaps

Missed zones, clogged heads, poor coverage, and heat stress can closely mimic chinch-bug injury—especially in full sun and near hard surfaces.

Mowing or chemical injury

Scalping, dull blades, spills, overlap, drift, or a recent product application can leave patterns that appear suddenly without turf-feeding insects.

Root and soil stress

Compaction, drainage, construction debris, buried material, thatch, shade, or root disease may weaken turf and alter how firmly it is anchored.

    Common questions

    Straight answers about lawn insects.

    If your question is not here, call the local Grow Green team at (225) 461-3199.

    How can I tell whether the damage is insects or fungus?

    Color and patch shape alone may not be enough. Chewed blades, visible insects, green pellets, spittle, tunnels, clipped roots, turf that lifts easily, and activity at the damaged edge can support an insect diagnosis. Weather, moisture, leaf lesions, root symptoms, and maintenance history help separate disease or environmental stress.

    How quickly can armyworms damage a lawn?

    During a heavy outbreak, armyworm larvae can remove foliage very quickly; LSU AgCenter notes that severe feeding may devastate turf overnight. Prompt inspection matters, but the amount of living crown and runner tissue left after feeding still determines recovery.

    Why do chinch bugs look so much like drought?

    Southern chinch bugs feed at the base of St. Augustinegrass and often injure hot, sunny, water-stressed areas first. The resulting yellow-to-brown patches can look like poor irrigation. Finding the insects near the active margin helps distinguish the two.

    Will damaged grass grow back after treatment?

    It may if enough living crowns, runners, and roots remain and growing conditions support recovery. Treatment does not turn dead tissue green. Severe areas may require more time, repair, or replacement even after insect pressure is reduced.

    Is lawn insect control included in the regular lawn program?

    Grow Green’s main lawn program includes seasonal planned visits per year, generally about six weeks apart. Insect attention depends on your specific plan, season, and activity found. A targeted follow-up or one-time insect treatment may be quoted separately; the team reviews that scope with you first.

    Will one treatment prevent every future lawn insect?

    No outdoor treatment permanently excludes every insect or life stage. Results depend on the target pest, pressure, life cycle, timing, weather, application site, and product label. Continued scouting may be needed when pressure remains favorable.

    When can children and pets return to the lawn?

    Keep people and pets out of the treatment area during application and until the product label’s re-entry directions have been satisfied. This often includes allowing treated surfaces to dry, but directions can vary. Grow Green provides the applicable instructions for your service.

    Do you handle fire ants, mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks too?

    Yes, but those are separate outdoor pest services. Use Fire Ant Treatment for mounds and colony pressure, or Mosquito, Flea & Tick Treatment for biting pests around outdoor-use areas. Choose “Not sure” in this form if you want the office to route the request.

    What areas do you serve?

features.title: Southern Chinch Bugs
features.body: Small sap-feeding insects strongly associated with St. Augustinegrass. Their injury can resemble drought and often begins in stressed, sunny areas.

features.title: Fall Armyworms
features.body: Caterpillars that feed on grass blades and can remove foliage rapidly during an outbreak. Most turfgrasses can be affected; bermudagrass is a common target in Louisiana.

features.title: Tropical Sod Webworms
features.body: Larvae feed on leaf tissue, often making affected turf appear unevenly clipped or scalped. St. Augustine, bermuda, and centipede are common hosts in Louisiana.

features.title: Mole Crickets
features.body: Some species feed on turf while tunneling can also loosen soil, dry roots, and disrupt the surface. Timing and life stage strongly affect treatment strategy.

features.title: An active outbreak does not have to wait for the next routine visit.

process.title: Tell us what changed
process.body: Share the grass type, where damage began, how fast it moved, what you see in the blades or soil, and anything already applied.

process.title: Inspect likely activity
process.body: We compare the injury with likely insects, disease, irrigation, mowing, and root stress. The active edge often receives the closest look.

process.title: Treat the target
process.body: When an actionable pest is present or strongly supported, we choose a labeled product and application approach appropriate for that pest and site.

process.title: Protect recovery
process.body: We explain watering, mowing, and monitoring steps. Follow-up depends on pest biology, life stage, pressure, weather, and surviving turf.
